📋PM Edition — What You Need to Know

“Small caps and the Dow rally as tech slips, but the junk-bond stress keeps creeping up toward better-rated borrowers”

🗒️What This Means For You
  • Fed Hike: Since the 2026-09-16 Fed hike the Treasury-rate leg of IG returns is -0.45% (intraday, 7-year +6bp). At trading day 24 (last close) it was -0.45% against a five-campaign average of -1.44% at the same point — 1994-95, 1999-00, 2022-23 were worse. The spread leg adds -0.63%. The 10-year is +9bp since the hike vs a +20bp campaign average at the same point. The 2s10s steepening may be topping (intraday 4 of 4 signals: topping likely).
  • HY Contagion: Junk-bond stress: the CCC-to-single-B spread gap is 762bp against a five-year average of 413bp (widest since Apr 2020). Better-rated junk is following: single-B +80bp and BB +52bp in a month. CCC and single-B are moving together more (correlation 0.30 → 0.61 over 3 months; five-year norm 0.70). Investment grade is moving too (+11bp in a month).
  • Bank Earnings: 9 banks reported (BOKF, FNB, WAL, WTFC, ZION, AUB, CBSH, KEY, UCB); 1 red-flagged (ZION: Coverage falling while NPLs rise (+7%, +$19mm)). Credit deteriorating at the margin; deposit costs flat. Watch: ZION.
  • Stocks: Small companies and the Dow rallied; tech-heavy Nasdaq was flat-to-down; fear gauge fell.
  • FX: Dollar slipped slightly; euro, yen and pound barely moved after the close.
  • Technicals: S&P barely above its 50-day average trend line; Nasdaq slipped below it.
  • Sectors: Investors are rotating out of tech into health care, staples and other defensive sectors.
  • Credit/Spreads: Junk-bond stress is spreading from the riskiest borrowers to stronger borrowers, though high-grade spreads are still tight.
  • Crisis: Overall stress is moderate; the biggest risks are the riskiest corporate borrowers and the oil shock.
  • Inflation: Core inflation is steady near 2.6-3%, but energy-driven prices are still running hot.
  • Tech Bubble: Valuations are far below 2000 levels, but complacency and easy credit look late-cycle.
  • Earnings & IPOs: Meta reports tomorrow; Bloom Energy carries the biggest expected swing; big IPOs abroad.
  • Iran: We found no verified new Iran news today; oil prices still carry a war premium.
  • Warsh: Warsh gives no advance guidance; a hold next week is our best guess.
  • Week Ahead: The Fed meets October 27-28; Q3 GDP and the PCE inflation report follow October 29.
  • Outlook: Neutral near term; cautious over the coming months as credit stress builds.
  • Trades: Own health care, cut junk bonds, trim Nasdaq, and buy 10-year Treasuries on a tactical basis.
  • Trades Vol: 45 watchlist names screened: 2 buy, 2 sell, 21 hold long, 20 stay out
  • Regime Rules: S&P 500 risk-on; NDX risk-on, 6.0% above its sell trigger; trend intact; credit spreads widening
  • Treasury Liquidity: Treasury liquidity/rates-vol monitor: TLT 95/100 put skew +0.59 vol pts, Fed DKW real term premium +91bp.
  • 10Y Pattern: 10Y at 93th pctile, +19bp from the 2026 rim — still compressing, not a cup-and-handle.
  • Diesel Futures: Diesel: 1-9 of 10 signals point lower.
  • Bottom line: Stocks look calm but junk-bond stress is spreading; keep risk light.

PM close, Tue Oct 20: a broadening, defensive-tilted rally. The S&P 500 rose 0.28% to 7712.57 and the Dow added 1.02% (+529.85) to 52495.88. Small caps led, with the Russell 2000 up 1.65% to 2773.42, while the Nasdaq Composite slipped 0.02% to 26424.82. The VIX fell 1.13 points to 17.31. Overseas it was a weaker session: Euro Stoxx 50 -0.38%, FTSE 100 -0.29% and Nikkei 225 -1.30%. Treasuries rallied at the long end: the 10Y fell 3.12bp to 5.1085% and the 30Y fell 4.75bp to 5.4198%, while the 2Y edged up to 4.7761%, flattening the curve. Brent remains elevated at 109.15. The biggest story is still underneath the surface, in junk credit. Bloomberg's Caa-minus-B spread gap is 750bp, against a 5-year average of 412bp. That is the 100th percentile of the past 5 years and the widest since 2020-04-24. Caa OAS is 1072bp, up 153bp in a month. The stress is moving up the quality ladder: single-B OAS rose 70bp in a month to 322bp, and Ba rose 48bp to 198bp. IG is up 10bp to 85bp but is still near historic tights (10th percentile all-time). The 63-day Caa/B correlation of daily spread changes has jumped from 0.27 a month ago to 0.61. That is still below its 0.70 5-year median, so contagion is building but not yet the normal lockstep. FRED's ICE CCC series (1297bp, 100th percentile) confirms the move. This is descriptive, not a validated signal. Meanwhile the headline HY OAS (3.29%) still looks benign, and that gap between the top-line index and the rot underneath is what we are watching. Sentiment is complacent at the index level (VIX lower, small caps bid) but defensive underneath: health care is +5.83% over the week while tech is -4.81%.

Two-sided analog episodes per signal: days where the signal's percentile-rank (vs its own full history) was <=5th or >=95th, or |z-score|>=1.3, clustered into one episode per zone per >=6-month gap between episode starts. For each zone, the realized forward 6-month % change in the BENCHMARK'S OUTRIGHT PRICE from each episode start is measured; a card's direction (BUY/SELL) is whichever sign that median historical move carries. Entry/target/stretch/stop are computed directly from this table -- the narrative prose (thesis/rationale) is the only part supplied by an LLM, and it is not permitted to alter a number. Crack spreads and curve shapes are, financially, relative-value signals rather than clean predictors of outright price; expressing every card in outright price terms is a deliberate simplification. HO36 Comdty (ULSD's 36-month point) is thin/less liquid on this seat -- treat its curve-shape reading with lower confidence than the others. Not investment advice.

Churn = the longest window of 20-120 sessions whose close range is <= 8x its median ATR(14), with median ADX(14) < 20, an insignificant close-price slope (p > 0.05), and >= 2 entries into each edge zone (top/bottom 20% of the band). Support/resistance = median swing low/high (+/-5 sessions); outer edges = the window's extreme closes. Breakout = a close beyond the outer edge by > 0.5 ATR, confirmed by a second close or one close beyond 1 ATR. A break back inside within 5 sessions is a failed break. An episode's outer edges can widen at most 0.5 ATR past their first detection, so a slow grind can't drag the range along with it. Base rates come from replaying the same rules over the full history, day by day, with no lookahead. This is pattern analysis of historical prices, not investment advice.

🔄Sector Analysis

The rotation is clearly defensive and out of growth. US 1-week: Health Care +5.83%, Cons Staples +3.95%, Materials +2.35%, Cons Discr +2.30% versus Info Tech -4.81% and Comm Services -4.13%. Over 1 month the defensive lean is sharper: Staples +7.55%, Health Care +6.23% and Energy +9.36%, against Tech -3.87% and Comm Services -4.68%. Global sectors confirm it: Tech -5.24% for the week and -5.32% for the month, Health Care +5.64% / +4.72%, Staples +4.32% / +6.74%. Today Health Care (+2.33%), Real Estate (+1.69%), Utilities (+1.15%) and Financials (+1.12%) led, while Tech (-0.34%) and Comm Services (-0.89%) lagged. YTD, Energy (+48.88% US) and Tech (+22.54% US) are still the big winners. The current pattern, long-duration growth sold and defensives plus energy bought, is typical of a late-cycle, high-yield, oil-shocked regime rather than an early-cycle broadening.

🧮Fixed Income Spreadscomputed

Headline spreads still look calm. US IG OAS is 0.85% (z -0.74, 10th percentile; 0% of the way to GFC, EuroDebt 2011, COVID or Hike-2022 crisis levels, computed). US HY OAS is 3.29% (z -0.64, 23rd percentile, 12% toward Hike-2022 levels). EUR IG is 0.98% (+3bp, 27th percentile) and EUR HY is 3.69% (+11bp, 41st percentile, 15% toward COVID). EM USD is 1.8% (z -1.20, 7th percentile). Beneath the HY headline, though, the quality ladder is cracking from the bottom. Caa is 1072bp (+153bp over 1 month, +274bp over 3 months), and the Caa-B gap is 750bp versus a 412bp 5-year average (100th percentile, widest since 2020-04-24). Single-B is +70bp over 1 month and Ba +48bp, so the stress is spreading upward. The B-Ba gap (124bp) and the HY-IG gap (244bp) are still near their 5-year averages (129bp and 240bp), however. Contagion therefore has not yet reached the BB/IG boundary in relative terms; it is showing up as a parallel lift in levels. Key levels: US HY OAS moving back above its ~3.5% 5-year-average zone would mean the headline index is catching up to the Caa damage. That would likely require single-B to climb toward ~3.5-4.0% and the Caa/B correlation to reclaim its 0.70 5-year median. US IG would need to break above ~1.0% to signal high-grade spillover, plausibly via a growth or earnings shock with the 10Y holding above 5%. All of this is descriptive, not a validated signal.

Widening velocity, not level. Near an all-time high a 63d widening past the trigger has historically raised P(SPX -10% within 3m) from ~8.6% to ~21.9% (Baa p=0.013, HY p=0.028, IG p=0.047, 1990-2026, corroborated on three independently-sourced series). The spread LEVEL carries no such signal once you control for already being in a drawdown (p=0.562) — tight spreads near a high are expected and are not reassurance. ARMED marks elevated tail RISK, not a sell: 78% of past ARMED episodes did not produce a 10% drawdown. 💧Treasury liquidity & rates volcomputed

US Govt Securities Liquidity Index (GVLQUSD), MOVE, Fed DKW term premium and TLT option skew, live from Bloomberg + federalreserve.gov.

Five charts tracking the mechanism Simon White laid out for why Treasury liquidity is deteriorating: rising inflation volatility feeds into a higher term premium, which steepens the curve, which raises bond vol, which shows up as worse UST market liquidity. Right now UST liquidity is at the 50th percentile of its own history (higher = worse) and the Fed's own DKW real term premium is +91bp.

Latest reading is +0.59 vol points (15th percentile of the 47 runs recorded so far). Positive means the 5%-OTM put is pricier than the at-the-money option -- the market paying up for downside-price / higher-yield insurance on long-end Treasuries.

UST liquidity index is 1.53 (50th percentile of its own 2007-present history -- 100th = worst liquidity on record), improving over the past 3 months (-0.08 pts). CPI YoY volatility (2yr) is 0.50pp; the article's thesis is that rising inflation vol drags liquidity worse, which this chart is built to let you check month to month.

Real term premium is +91bp (96th percentile of its own 2007-present history), up 12bp over the trailing ~2 months. Inflation risk premium is +14bp. Fed staff's own DKW decomposition (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei) splits the rise in long yields into a policy-uncertainty component (real term premium) and an inflation-uncertainty component -- both rising is the article's read that this move isn't just a rate-expectations story.

MOVE is 101.7 (73th percentile of its own post-2007 history). The 3m10s curve is 93bp (steeper by 12bp over 3 months). The article's claim is mechanical, not just correlated -- a steeper curve gives forward rates more room to move before converging to spot, which is itself higher realized/implied vol.

MOVE and the UST liquidity index have moved together with a full-history correlation of +0.72 (both series read as 'worse' when they rise). That's the closing link in the article's chain: inflation vol -> term premium -> curve steepness -> bond vol -> liquidity.

Recreates 5 charts from Bloomberg MacroScope, 'Treasury Market Liquidity Is a Live Issue Again' (Simon White, 19-Aug-2026). TLT skew accumulates one point per report run -- Bloomberg's option-surface field is snapshot-only, not retrievable historically via the API. Term premium is the Fed's own DKW model series (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei), pulled directly from federalreserve.gov, not Bloomberg. Not a trading signal -- a liquidity/vol monitor only.

Retracement of the left-rim decline: 76% (needs ≥90% to pass). 10Y level that passes: 6.16% (105bp above today).
Retracement = (right rim − cup base) / (left rim − cup base) = (5.30 − 0.51) / (6.79 − 0.51) = 76%.
Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base) = 0.51 + 0.90 × (6.79 − 0.51) = 6.16%.

Same test on each trailing window: cup base = lowest close in the window, left rim = highest close before it, right rim = highest close after it. Cup complete at ≥90% retracement; above 110% the yield has run past the old high (a breakout, not a cup). No cup inside the window when its left rim is not the highest close of the 91 days before it, i.e. yields were already falling into the window. Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base).

🗞️Street View — Where the Cycle Is HeadingCURATED · AS OF 2026-10-01

⚠ Commentary is 19 days old (as of 2026-10-01); it may not reflect the latest Fed news.

Consensus is a short, shallow campaign: one or two more 25bp hikes, December more likely than October. The debate is whether hiking into an energy shock ends in recession, and the bond market is already doing some of the tightening.

The Fed

  • Sept 16: unanimous 25bp hike to 3.75–4.00%, the first since 2023. Dots: median one more hike in 2026; 16 of 18 see at least one, 4 see two. Inflation not back at 2% until 2029. (CNBC, FedAndMarkets)
  • Warsh's message was distinctly hawkish (inflation 'too high and broad-based'); the Conference Board calls it 'not a one and done'. (Conference Board)
  • Sept 29, Williams (NY Fed): 'no need for urgency'; one more hike 'late this year' may be appropriate; the biggest inflation shocks have passed. (Bloomberg, NY Fed)
  • Sept 30, August PCE came in soft: headline 3.4% (vs 3.7% expected), core 3.0% (vs 3.3%). October odds fell; December still priced. Kashkari: inflation 'still too high'. (CNBC, CNBC (Kashkari))

Market pricing

  • October 28 hike odds vary widely by venue, roughly 35% to 69% (prediction markets highest, CME futures ~58%), mostly measured before the soft PCE print. (PredictionMarketsPicks)
  • About 83% odds of another hike by year-end; futures price ~93bp of tightening over the next 9 meetings, more than the dots. (Forbes)

Bonds and credit

  • 10-year Treasury above 5.25% (Sept 28), the highest since 2007; 30-year ~5.49%. Drivers cited: sticky energy inflation (Iran war), heavy issuance, AI capex demand. Term premium ~1.0–1.4%. (CNBC, CNBC (Warsh's yield problem))
  • AI-related issuers trade ~115bp vs ~78bp for IG overall; high-yield AI supply $40B year to date vs $12B in all of 2025. BNP and Goldman warn the issuance could pressure spreads. (Reuters, Bloomberg (BNP))

The bear case

  • Rosenberg: the Fed has never hiked into an energy shock without a recession, and AI won't save it this time. (TheStreet)
  • Goldman called the case for hiking 'weak' (demand not overheating, energy inflation should fade when the war ends). Oxford Economics: 'The Fed cannot control energy prices'; the risk is a weaker labor market. (CNN)

Read-through: For bonds, the bigger risk is the long end, not the Fed: term premium and supply keeping the 10-year above 5% matter more than one extra 25bp. The recession call is loud but isn't in any sell-side house view yet.

Curated summary of published Fed, market and economist commentary (news and research via the web), not a computed series and not a forecast. Odds differ by venue and move daily.

🔥Is Inflation Persistent?

Persistence score: 58/100 — Sticky but not re-accelerating at the core. Underlying measures are clustered around 2.2-2.8%: Median CPI 2.61, Trimmed-Mean CPI 2.66, Median PCE 2.57, Trimmed-Mean PCE 2.19, Core Sticky CPI 2.78. Most are flat-to-falling, and the computed core-trend sub-score sits in the middle of its history. The problem is breadth and energy. Flexible CPI is 6.12% and rising, and the Dallas Fed distribution shows 28.9% of the PCE basket rising faster than 5% (13.2% above 10%), even as 25.8% of the basket is outright falling. Headline Core PCE is 3.01%, still about a point above target. The verdict is an energy-driven, two-speed inflation that keeps the Fed from easing but does not demand hikes on core trends alone.

Bubble-analog — today's Nasdaq vs the dot-com cycle (two anchors)

WHY TWO START DATES?
Each line is rebased to 100 at a low the tech bull launched from, so elapsed time lines up. Oct-2022 is today's anchor — it was the prior bear-market bottom. Oct-1990 is the dot-com cycle's equivalent (its literal prior bear bottom). But 1990 predates the internet mania by ~4 years, so the second chart re-anchors the dot-com line to the 1994 reset low, just before the surge ignited, for a tighter like-for-like. Today sits very early under the strict 1990 analog, further along under the 1994 surge analog.
━ Anchored at the prior bear-market bottom (Oct-1990)   ━ today's cycle
━ Anchored at the pre-internet reset low (1994)   ━ today's cycle

Valuation marker: today's Nasdaq P/E (42x) ≈ 24% of the ~175x 2000-peak P/E.

IF THIS RHYMES WITH 2000
Nasdaq fell -78.0% peak→trough (2000-03-10 → 2002-10-09, ~31 months); it took ~15 years to reclaim the high.

The current Nasdaq path, anchored at Oct-2022, is at 240.5 after 48 months. The dot-com path anchored at Oct-1990 did not peak until month 113 at 1423.9, so on a price-path basis today's run is far less extreme. The concern is not a valuation blow-off but a cycle that has been running on tight credit and low volatility while the bottom of the credit ladder rots. The analyst-estimate inputs place today in elevated but not mania territory: S&P top-10 concentration ~40%, CAPE ~38x, market-cap/GDP ~215%, IPO froth ~55/100 (mega-deals abroad and a reported Anthropic marketing window of the week of Nov 9), and long-term EPS growth expectations ~65/100. These were not web-verified this run and are judgement estimates. Tech's 1-week -4.81% while defensives rally is what a late-cycle rotation looks like, not a blow-off top.

🏦Fed Chair Warsh
NEAR TERM

Next FOMC is October 27-28 (decision Oct 28, 2:00 PM ET). Inference: a hold is the most likely outcome. Warsh has refused forward guidance and avoided pre-committing; core PCE at 3.01% blocks cuts, while contained median/trimmed-mean measures and falling long yields reduce the urgency to hike. Hike risk is not trivial, given his late-July press conference left open his willingness to raise rates against stubborn inflation. Probability judgement: analyst estimate.

~1 YEAR

Inference from his record: (1) Less communication and no forward guidance, so expect more market volatility around meetings. (2) He has framed the 'big questions' around AI-driven productivity, demographics and the Iran-war shock. That suggests he could justify easing later if productivity disinflation shows up, but only after the energy impulse fades. (3) His long-standing views favour a smaller Fed balance sheet. Base case over ~1 year (analyst estimate): policy stays restrictive near term, with eventual cuts conditional on oil retreating and core PCE moving toward 2.5%. The long-standing balance-sheet view is from his record and was not re-verified in this run's sources.

Reporting from late August describes Warsh as communicating much less than his predecessors, declining forward guidance on the grounds that it limits flexibility, and leaving markets unsure after his July presser. The 30Y Treasury yield then hit a 19-year high the following week. One source cited US inflation at 4.2% in May. For Jackson Hole, Warsh said he wanted to focus on AI and productivity, demographics, and the global response to the Iran-war shock. We did not retrieve coverage of what he actually said there, so we do not characterize it.
